visible.summary: Cabo Verde is workable — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex relations legal and employment discrimination prohibited — no partner-related exposure for visitors.
visible.localsOnly: No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear) — resident-facing gaps.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR statute absent; evidence base thin but consistent.

sources.claim: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex union recognition; LGBTIQ orgs register freely; first public Pride 2013 (second African country); 2019–21 polls: 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour; Cabo Verde one of two African UN LGBTI Core Group members, made 2024 UPR anti-discrimination commitments.

Equal Eyes (20 Jul 2018): 2018 Pride Week in Praia — parade plus NGO campaigns (Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia, Associação Arco Iris) petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged.

Observador/Lusa (11 Jul 2017): PM Ulisses Correia e Silva said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020): 'All in this together' - Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe stand out as particularly tolerant countries; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Rede Angola interview (22 Jun 2016) with Tchinda Andrade, first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde (came out 1997, age 19): describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

visible.summary: São Tomé and Príncipe demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2012; small, peaceful, tourism-growing islands; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; thin community.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2012 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: Everything Explained summary: legal since 2012; equal age of consent 18 since 2021 (Law 15/2021, previously 16); no relationship recognition or adoption; Labour Code 2019 Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition.

Under the Penal Code in force since November 2012 same-sex conduct is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Labour Code (2019) Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation, and Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) allows enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred. No same-sex marriages, civil unions or partnerships are recognised; a 2016 poll found 46% of Sao Tomeans would not mind an LGBTQ neighbour.

Wikipedia-derived page updated 25 Apr 2026: same-sex conduct legal since the November 2012 Penal Code with equal age of consent 16; no recognition of same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. The page lists no general anti-discrimination protection (the 2019 Labour Code employment ban is not reflected here) and records the country among UN Joint Statement signatories on sexual orientation and gender identity.

visible.summary:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 8 years, 100 lashes available) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners, and the operative law on any local island.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Resort islands are de-facto insulated; the score reflects the national legal framework and local-island exposure.

sources.claim: HRMI Maldives Summary Report 2024 (second expert survey): human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political participation scores relatively better at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower.

Erasing 76 Crimes (1 September 2015): police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men (aged 56 and 27) on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 Penal Code extended criminalisation beyond Muslims to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; Rainbow Warriors warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN OHCHR compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015) for the Maldives’ second-cycle UPR: records ICCPR/CEDAW/CRC reservations and concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage; the Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Maldives national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015): the government’s own submission — of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons; reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years.

visible.summary: Sierra Leone is dangerous for trans visitors. The 1861 Offences Against the Person Act criminalises buggery with up to life imprisonment (men only) — enforcement is limited but discrimination and violence are regular; no LGR; a small community organises quietly.
visible.tangentialFactors: Buggery criminalised (up to life imprisonment, men only, limited enforcement) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sierra Leone's criminalisation of same-sex activity (up to life imprisonment under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act).

Amnesty International Sierra Leone 2025 country report (LGBTI section): consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, but lesbian women face significant social, cultural and economic barriers to living freely — stigma, harassment, and limited acceptance from families and communities; no non-discrimination protection for SOGI is documented.

Joint ICCPR shadow report (March 2014) to the UN Human Rights Committee: 'Breaking the Silence on Human Rights Violations in Sierra Leone' - discrimination and violence based on SOGI; covers civil-war sexual violence, discrimination in health and education, hate speech by religious institutions, and hate crimes against LGBTI human-rights defenders.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Sierra Leone: documents police killings, corruption, FGM/C, and 'official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals'.

GlobalGayz news archive for Sierra Leone (Richard Ammon, items dated 2004-2010): records the November 2004 rape and murder of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy, the January 2005 arrest of her killer, police refusal to classify it as a hate crime, and the alleged murderer's reported escape from custody in July 2005 — dated evidence on violence against LGBT activists and the justice response.

visible.summary: Kosovo is workable for trans visitors — the Balkans' strongest legal framework on paper. The constitution (Art 24) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covers gender identity; legal gender recognition is possible (medicalised); and the government attempted same-sex unions in 2024 as part of Council of Europe accession. Counterweights: implementation is inconsistent, political hate speech is common (2022 CSGD report: year marked by intolerance), and Pristina Pride proceeds under protection.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2024 same-sex unions attempt — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; not yet law.
visible.localsOnly: The medicalised LGR process is resident-facing; the implementation gaps affect resident victims.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: De jure unit: scored separately from Serbia per boundaries. Implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright overview (upd. Mar 2026): constitutional ban on SO discrimination (art. 24) plus the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; PM Kurti's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of Feb 2026 Parliament still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition including from the ruling party.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (May 2024) covers Muslim-majority Kosovo considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Kosovo: PM Kurti said during Pride week he would 'do his utmost' to get the Civil Code adopted (2022 parliament had voted against same-sex-couple recognition amendments); a Justice Ministry working group was drafting a bill; CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during Civil Code debates; an artist received death threats over a painting; Kosovo Pride Week held with the motto 'I love you as you are!'.

Prishtina Insight (Jan 2019): ECtHR ruled Macedonia's surgery requirement for gender-marker change violates private-life rights (X v FYROM); Kosovo's Blert Morina — who has his own Constitutional Court case on name/gender change on Kosovo IDs — watched the ruling closely, documenting that Kosovo's legal gender recognition route ran through the courts at that time.
Euronews (March 2022): Kosovo's parliament rejected the new law recognising same-sex civil unions (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

Prishtina Insight: third annual Pride Parade in Prishtina, with week-long exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions by the Center for Equality and Liberty (CEL) — slogan both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade; visible, public LGBTI organising in the capital.

IntelliNews: 'Kosovo's new Civil Code opens the way for gay marriage' - analysis of the Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language and its implications (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

visible.summary: Gambia is dangerous for trans visitors. There is no LGR and no visible community.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Criminal Code criminalises same-sex conduct, the 2014 amendment added an “aggravated homosexuality” offence (life imprisonment for “serial offenders”), and in 2024 the National Assembly raised the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to 5 years — the trajectory is towards harsher penalties, not reform. Under Jammeh, LGBTI people faced documented persecution (his infamous “slit throats” rhetoric); the Barrow era has seen some improvement in general freedoms but no decriminalisation and continued severe discrimination (Freedom House). Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.

sources.claim: Outright International country profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised since the colonial era; the 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' life clause was removed by the March 2025 Criminal Code, which instead sets a five-year minimum for 'unnatural offences' (defined as any homosexual act) with no stated maximum, plus three years for 'gross indecency'; the Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions.

West Africa Democracy Radio: reports The Gambia's new criminal-law package raising the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to five years — broadcast corroboration of the penalty change now on the books.

Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2024: The Gambia rated 'Partly Free' (50/100); political freedoms improved under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule, with severe discrimination against LGBT+ people listed among ongoing concerns.

UK Home Office CPIN on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia (v3.0, Feb 2023): systematic assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information on law and treatment — the fullest English-language documentation of conditions on the ground.

HRW report 'State of Fear' (Sept 2015): arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in Gambia under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people — the enforcement climate of the previous regime, relevant to how police treat visibly LGBT visitors.
US State Dept 2020 human-rights report on Gambia: same-sex conduct criminalised (up to life under the 2013 amendment); documents arrests and societal discrimination.
US State Dept 2021 report: continued criminalisation with no prosecutions reported; significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons.
